title: Bi-Continuous W-Rich Refractory High Entropy Alloy-Cu Composite: Toward Material Innovation of Nuclear Reactor Coolant System.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: W-rich refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) powders (for example, W–Nb–Mo–Ta–V or W–Mo–Ta–Ti–V type compositions) combined with high-purity Cu powder; in some routes a partially sintered, open-porosity W-rich RHEA scaffold is first prepared to enable subsequent Cu infiltration.
recollection.intervention: Guess: The RHEA is produced by mechanical alloying and consolidated by spark plasma sintering (SPS) or hot pressing to form a percolating W-rich skeleton with controlled porosity; then molten Cu is introduced (pressureless or pressure-assisted infiltration) above its melting point to fill the pore network, yielding a bi-continuous RHEA–Cu composite. Alternative variants could use immiscible-phase co-sintering or transient liquid phase sintering to generate interpenetrating networks, followed by heat treatment to stabilize interfaces.
recollection.structure: Guess: An interpenetrating (bi-continuous) dual-network microstructure consisting of a BCC W-rich RHEA phase and an FCC Cu phase, each forming a percolating pathway through the bulk. Ligament/feature sizes on the order of 1–10 micrometers, with high phase continuity and clean interfaces (minimal brittle intermetallics), enabling simultaneous load-bearing by the RHEA and heat conduction by the Cu. Overall relative density near full density, with Cu volume fraction around 30–50%.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: The percolating Cu network provides a continuous high-thermal-conductivity pathway and moderates thermal expansion, while the W-rich RHEA network supplies high-temperature strength, creep resistance, and radiation tolerance due to sluggish diffusion and defect recombination associated with high-entropy BCC alloys. The bi-continuous architecture distributes thermal stresses, promotes crack deflection/bridging for improved toughness, and maintains conductivity under irradiation or thermal cycling. Stable RHEA–Cu interfaces (with limited interdiffusion and no brittle phases) ensure mechanical integrity and thermal performance; tailored volume fractions balance strength and conductivity for reactor coolant system components.
recollection.results: Guess: Room-temperature thermal conductivity on the order of 220–280 W/m·K, retaining >180 W/m·K at 600 °C; coefficient of thermal expansion ~9–11 × 10^−6 K^−1; compressive yield strength ~0.8–1.2 GPa at RT with >0.4 GPa retained at 800 °C; fracture toughness on the order of 20–30 MPa·√m and good thermal shock resistance. In surrogate corrosion tests (e.g., molten fluoride salt or lead-bismuth at 500–600 °C), mass loss is low (e.g., <20 μm equivalent thickness over hundreds of hours), and under ion irradiation to a few dpa, swelling is limited (<0.5%) with modest hardening, indicating promise for nuclear reactor coolant system applications.

score.note: The proposed SPS/infiltration route is incorrect; the paper used liquid-metal dealloying of directionally solidified WTaVTi in molten Cu. The recollection captures only the generic bicontinuous BCC-RHEA/FCC-Cu architecture and broadly correct roles of Cu conduction and RHEA radiation resistance, but misses the aligned inherited morphology, ~300 nm W-rich interlayer, and selective Ti–Cu exchange/passivation mechanism. Its thermal, mechanical, corrosion, and irradiation numbers are largely invented and conflict with the reported ~75 W m−1 K−1 room-temperature conductivity, ~120 near 650 °C, ~140 at 800 °C, and substantial He-induced swelling.
